nodes.question: How does soil condition affect tire inflation pressure?
nodes.answer: In softer soil conditions, tire inflation pressure may be reduced compared to the recommended pressure for the same load on firmer surfaces because the soil deforms to increase the contact patch area and thus reduce tire deflection.
nodes.paragraph: With an increasing load on the tire, the in ation pressure must be raised to maintain acceptable de ections, avoid damage tothe tire and for safety reasons. In soft (off-road) conditions, the soil deforms to allow for increased contact patch area, thus reducing the de ection of the tire for a given load and in ation pressure [ 3]. Hence, in softer soil conditions, the tire in ation pressure may be reduced compared with therecommended pressure for the same load on a rmer sur- face. Central tire in ation systems (CTIS) offer advantages for quick adjustments of the tires in ation pressure forimproved traction, reduced slip and tire wear, and increased tire-soil contact area (equally, reduced soil-tire contact pressure). Such adjustments may help to reducerolling resistance, that is the pull required to move a wheel across a horizontal surface [ 2], and improve fuel use ef - ciency depending on speci C ground conditions, but therecommended tire in ation pressure must be restored for rmer surface use. Rolling resistance increases almost proportionally to the increase in load which the tire is supporting.

nodes.question: How does off-road rolling resistance compare to internal rolling resistance?
nodes.answer: In off-road conditions, the rolling resistance caused by soil deformation is about 5 times greater than the internal rolling resistance, depending upon the tire construction.
nodes.paragraph: The rolling resistance has two main compo-nents [ 50]: The internal rolling resistance, which is caused by the loss of energy resulting from the continuous exing of the tire S carcass as the wheel rotates in contact with the ground, and The external rolling resistance, which arises from the energy that the wheel must expend in deforming the soil surface. In off-road conditions, the rolling resistance caused by soil deformation is about 5 times greater (or more) than theinternal resistance, depending upon the tire construction. If weight cannot be reduced, an increase in the contact area will reduce the soil-tire contactpressure. A reduction in the contact pressure can be achieved by increasing the tire diameter, the section width or both (although the former is preferable to keep rollingresistance low), operating the tire at the minimum allow- able (safe) in ation pressure or tting dual tires at low in ation pressure, and where possible, using repeatedwheeling [ 63].

nodes.question: What processes can affect the spatial configurations of air-filled pore space in soil?
nodes.answer: Spatial configurations of air-filled pore space can be affected by biotic processes like bioturbation, abiotic processes like wetting and drying cycles, or technical processes like tillage.
nodes.paragraph: 2010; Silvennoinen et al. 2008; Veraart et al. 2011; Werner et al. 2014; Zhu et al. 2013). The total oxygen supply and demand in soil is hetero - geneously distributed. Even if the overall water content and substrate availability are the same, the denitrification rates and kinetics can be very different depending on the spatial distribution patterns of microbial hotspots (Schl ter et al. 2019; Zhu et al. 2015). Denitrification hotspots are typically formed around decomposing plant residues (H jberg et al. 1994; Kravchenko et al. 2017; Parkin 1987), and sometimes almost all N2O production can originate from a very small fraction of the soil volume (Parkin 1987). The distribution patterns of air-filled pores and organic residues are not ran- dom, but are imposed by soil structure. That is, the air-filled pore space at a given matric potential can have different spa- tial configurations depending on how the pores were formed, e.g. by biotic processes like bioturbation, abiotic processes like wetting drying cycles or technical processes like tillage.

nodes.question: What was the bulk density of the grassland soil compared to the cropland soil?
nodes.answer: The bulk density of the grassland soil was lower at 1.0 g cm-3, while the bulk density of the cropland soil was 1.3 g cm-3.
nodes.paragraph: The soil is regularly ploughed to a depth of 30 cm and labelled as cropland in the following. The second soil was sampled from a grassland research station in Gie en and referred to as grassland (latitude N50 32 , longitude E8 41 , elevation 172 m a.s.l.). The soil was a flu - vic Gleysol with a clay loam texture, soil organic carbon contents of 4.42% and a pH of 6.71. The soil organic matter (SOM) content of the grassland soil was higher (4.46%) and the bulk density lower (1.0 g cm-3) compared to the cropland soil with SOC contents of 1.21% and a bulk density of 1.3 g cm-3, respectively (Rohe et al. 2021 ). More details about the field site can be found in Rohe et al. ( 2021 ). During sampling in late summer of 2022, a custom-made drill for undisturbed sampling of cylindrical soil cores (UGT GmbH, Germany) was used to take undisturbed samples (encased in a stiff 5 mm PE sleeve, Fig. 1). On each field site, five undis - turbed cores (10 cm height, 10 cm ) were taken from 5 to 15 cm depth.

nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How does the use of automatic spindle pickers during cotton fibre picking affect the soil quality?
nodes.answer: The use of automatic spindle pickers during cotton fibre picking can affect soil quality through processes like compaction and disruption of soil structure.
